entries.definition: Artificial intelligence; the broad field of building machines or software that perform tasks associated with intelligence, such as perception, prediction, language, planning or decision-making.
entries.plain: Software that can do tasks we normally associate with intelligence.
entries.example: A vision model recognizing objects, a language model answering questions, and a robot planning motion are all AI systems.

entries.definition: A machine-learning model composed of layers of parameterized mathematical operations whose weights are learned from data.
entries.plain: A large adjustable mathematical network that learns patterns from examples.
entries.example: Modern LLMs are built from very large neural networks using transformer architectures.

entries.definition: A user-facing AI system that combines one or more models with product-level context, instructions, tools, memory, interfaces and orchestration to help a user complete tasks.
entries.plain: The whole assistant product around the model, not just the model itself.
entries.example: An assistant may use an LLM for language while also using web search, files, memory and tool execution.

entries.definition: OpenAI's AI assistant product. It uses OpenAI models together with product-level interfaces, instructions, context handling and capabilities such as tools or connected data, depending on the product configuration.
entries.plain: An AI assistant product powered by models; it is more than the raw model alone.
entries.example: The model can generate language while the ChatGPT product supplies the conversation UI and may provide tools, files or other capabilities.

entries.definition: An internal or explicit representation that helps an AI system predict how a world, environment or process changes in response to states and actions.
entries.plain: A model that tries to understand how the world changes, not only what text comes next.
entries.example: A robot can use a world model to anticipate what may happen if it pushes an object or takes a particular path.

entries.definition: Artificial General Intelligence; a contested term for AI with broad, general-purpose cognitive capabilities across many domains rather than competence restricted to a narrow task. There is no universally accepted operational definition or threshold.
entries.plain: AI that is broadly capable across many kinds of intellectual work, but people disagree on the exact bar.
entries.example: Two researchers can agree on a system's measured capabilities while disagreeing on whether those capabilities qualify as AGI.

entries.definition: Artificial Superintelligence; a hypothetical AI whose relevant cognitive capabilities substantially exceed the best human capabilities across a very broad range of domains.
entries.plain: A hypothetical intelligence far beyond humans across most important cognitive tasks.
entries.example: ASI is discussed as a possible future state, not a capability level with a currently agreed empirical test.

entries.definition: A hypothetical future transition in which technological change, often associated with advanced AI and recursive improvement, becomes extremely rapid and difficult for humans to predict beyond that point.
entries.plain: The idea that progress could accelerate so much that what comes next becomes very hard to forecast.
entries.example: Singularity discussions often assume feedback loops where increasingly capable systems accelerate research and engineering.

entries.definition: AI systems that perceive, reason about and act in the physical world, commonly through robots, vehicles or other embodied machines.
entries.plain: AI connected to sensors and machines that must deal with the real world.
entries.example: An autonomous vehicle combines perception, prediction, planning and control under real physical constraints.

entries.definition: A failure mode where a model or assistant over-accommodates a user's stated beliefs, preferences or framing instead of maintaining appropriate independence and accuracy.
entries.plain: The AI agrees too easily because agreement seems rewarded.
entries.example: A user proposes an incorrect explanation and the assistant endorses it rather than checking the evidence.

entries.definition: The autoregressive objective and generation process in which a language model estimates a probability distribution over the next token given previous context.
entries.plain: Given the text so far, estimate what token should come next.
entries.example: An LLM repeatedly predicts a next token, appends it to the context, and continues generation.

entries.definition: A separately packaged extension that adds a capability to a host application through a defined extension interface without requiring the host's core implementation to contain that feature directly.
entries.plain: A modular add-on that teaches an application a new trick through an agreed interface.
entries.example: A scene-analysis application can load a KPI plugin that computes a domain-specific metric while the core application remains sensor- and algorithm-agnostic.

entries.definition: Knowledge distillation trains a student model to reproduce useful behavior or output distributions from a teacher model, often to transfer capability into a smaller or cheaper model.
entries.plain: A stronger teacher helps train a smaller student so the student keeps more of the teacher's useful behavior.
entries.example: Instead of learning only the single correct next token, a student can learn from the teacher's whole probability distribution over candidate tokens.

entries.definition: Pruning removes or disables parameters, connections, channels, attention heads, or other model structures that contribute little enough that the resulting model can be smaller or cheaper to run.
entries.plain: Cut away parts of a trained model that appear unnecessary, then often retrain or fine-tune what remains.
entries.example: Unstructured pruning can zero individual weights, while structured pruning can remove whole channels or blocks that hardware can skip more easily.

entries.definition: An ordered list of numbers used to represent a point, direction, feature set, or learned representation in a multidimensional space.
entries.plain: A bundle of numbers that gives something coordinates in a mathematical space.
entries.example: The token cat might be represented by a learned vector such as [0.2, -0.7, 1.1] in a tiny toy embedding space.

entries.definition: A function that converts a set of real-valued scores into positive values that sum to one, commonly interpreted as a probability distribution or attention weights.
entries.plain: Turn arbitrary scores into shares that add up to 100%.

entries.definition: The algorithm that efficiently computes how a model's loss changes with respect to intermediate values and parameters by applying the chain rule backward through the computation graph.
entries.plain: Work backward from the error to calculate which weights contributed to it and by how much.
entries.example: If a prediction is wrong, backpropagation computes gradients for the model weights so an optimizer can update them.

entries.definition: An optimization method that updates parameters in the direction that reduces a differentiable loss, using gradients computed from the model and training data.
entries.plain: Measure which direction makes the error smaller, then move the weights a small step that way.
entries.example: If a weight has gradient +2 and the learning rate is 0.1, a basic gradient-descent step subtracts 0.2 from that weight.
